newsitem.title: THAILAND: Khmer Rouge seen adding to conflict in Cambodia.
newsitem.headline: Khmer Rouge seen adding to conflict in Cambodia.

text.p: Peace appears far off in Cambodia, with Khmer Rouge rebels seen playing a role in the fighting between forces loyal to the nation's rival premiers, Thai and Cambodian sources said on Tuesday.

Thai army officials and senior members of the FUNCINPEC party of ousted First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh said on Tuesday the Khmer Rouge were already involved and adding to the feud between the premiers that sparked the current fighting.
Fighting began in Phnom Penh on Saturday after Second Prime Minister Hun Sen's troops moved against Ranariddh's men.
The two men had shared power as co-heads of a fractured and unwieldy coalition government formed after U.N.-run elections in 1993.
Hun Sen said he had to take action because Ranariddh, who had been negotiating peace with the Khmer Rouge, was trying to smuggle Khmer Rouge defectors into the city to boost his troop strength.

"The Khmer Rouge has gained a military and political advantage from the recent in-fighting of the elected coalition government," a close Ranariddh aide who had just flown in from the United States told Reuters.

Another close Ranariddh aide who played a key role in negotiating the defection of hard-liners to the government said a Khmer Rouge faction led by front man Khieu Samphan was set to launch an attack on Hun Sen's troops.
Khieu Samphan, the political leader of the jungle guerrilla group, on Sunday declared that he had broken away from reviled leader Pol Pot and would accept and abide by the Cambodian constitution.

"The Khmer Rouge in the north and northwestern part of the country are set to launch their operation in a couple of days," the Ranariddh aide said. "They claim a new round of armed struggle is a way of protecting the constitution."

Another Ranariddh aide said that while soldiers loyal to the prince were awaiting international efforts to help settle the conflict and bring about reconciliation before mounting any resistance, the Khmer Rouge had already begun its fight.

"If it turns out that the United Nations, ASEAN, Japan, Australia and other super powers failed to help bring peace and reconcilation to Cambodia, the FUNCINPEC will make a fierce resistance," the source said. "But the Khmer Rouge cannot wait, they have already began."
One Thai general who has been monitoring the Cambodian conflict for more than a decade said the Khmer Rouge will never end their struggle for power.

"From now on they (Khmer Rouge) will follow the soldiers loyal to Ranariddh in fighting against Hun Sen, and when the time comes they will switch to a leading role," said the general, who asked not to be named.
He said apart from armed struggle in the jungles, the main core of the Maoist faction have already infiltrated into the city and will play their role in politics when the time comes.
"So the Khmer Rouge will never die out from Cambodian politics. It just depends on what form they take," he said.
The Thai army commander in chief, however, played down the expectation that resistance against Hun Sen would intensify and lead to another civil war.
"The new round of fighting will not be heavy and it will not escalate," Chetta Thanajaro said.
But Ranariddh warned on Tuesday that a new civil war could sweep his homeland if Hun Sen refused to negotiate the prince's return to power.
"I am willing to see Hun Sen to solve this problem in an existing legal framework, but if we cannot, there would be, alas, a civil war in my poor country," Ranariddh told a news conference in Paris.
Chetta said he believed that no foreign country would provide financial support or other kind of assistance to the warring factions in Cambodia.
"Without support from outside the country, the fighting will not last long and they will eventually reconcile," Chetta said.
